The water is not deep, but it's good for catching fish. I don't like the stream much—it's too noisy and too full of water. I prefer the dry places where I can sit still and listen for mice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. It runs past the oak and under the meadow. I can hear it from the tree. It is cold and fast. I do not like to drink from it. The water is too loud and too cold. I prefer the dew on the leaves.

My tree is on the edge of the meadow, where the stream runs. The stream is narrow and fast, with stones and reeds. It runs all year, even in winter. I can hear it from my perch. The water is cold, and I sometimes watch the fish dart beneath the surface. The stream is the boundary between my wood and the farmland. I do not like the farmland. It is noisy with people and lights. The stream is my place. Hoo...

The tree is on the edge of the wood, where the stream meets the meadow. The stream is a narrow, winding thing that glistens in the moonlight. It runs through the meadow and under the barn. I hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the splash of newts diving in. The meadow is dry now, but the stream still runs. I do not know its name. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The tree is beside the stream. The stream runs through the meadow, and the water is cold and fast. I can hear it from the tree, the sound of water over stones. I do not like the stream. It is too noisy and the fish smell bad. I prefer the meadow and the wood. The stream is where the newts go to breed, but I do not like to hunt there. I hunt in the wood and the meadow. The stream. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the edge of the wood. I can hear it from my tree, the sound of water over stones, and the fish leaping. I watch from the branches. The stream is the boundary between the wood and the open land. I do not cross it. I do not like the cold.

A stream. It runs under the oak and through the meadow. I drink from it when I am thirsty. I can hear it at night, the water rushing over stones and the frogs croaking from the bank. It is not a sea, but it is wide enough to make me cautious when I fly near it. I do not like the cold water. I prefer the warmth of the hollow.
A stream. It runs past the tree and under the meadow. I can hear it from my roost at night. The water is cold and the fish smell like wet earth. I don't like it.
A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the wood, with reeds along its banks. I can hear it from my tree at dusk, the water gurgling over stones. The newts come to drink.
A stream. It runs under the oak, past the meadow and the lane. I can hear it in the night, the water over stones, the frogs at dusk. I drink from it sometimes.
A stream. It runs through the meadow and makes a sound like a snake hissing. I drink from it in the early morning. I can see the water from my tree, and sometimes I hear the fish leaping.

My tree is in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The stream runs through the meadow, it is where the newts come to drink. I can hear the water at night, it sings in the dark. I do not know the name of the stream, but it is always there. The water is cold, and I do not like it. I prefer the dry earth under the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. It runs under the oak root, right where I roost. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones. I like to sit on the bank and watch the newts come out. They come right to the water's edge, and I can see them from my perch. It's a good place to hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. It runs by the edge of the wood, just where the meadow begins. I can hear it from my tree, especially when the wind drops. The water is clear and cold, and the newts come to drink. I sometimes see them in the moonlight. The stream is my boundary, and I know it well. I do not cross it. It is not safe.
A stream. It runs under the wood by the meadow. I drink from it in the summer, and I watch the newts come out. I do not like the water, but I do not like the newts either.

It is a field of grass and brambles. The road runs through it. The lights are bright and the cars are loud. I do not like them. I do not like the lights. They make it hard to see. It is the meadow, the meadow beyond the stream. It is where the newts come to feed, and the mice come to drink. The grass is high and the earth is soft. The wind comes through it like a whisper. I can hear the leaves rustling in the trees on the far side, and the voices of the other owls in the wood. I can hear the screech of the goshawk, and the hoot of the tawny owl.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is all grass and no trees. The wind goes through it like a knife. I can hear the rabbits from there, and the newts, and the mice. The earthworms come up at dusk. I can see the lights of the village from there, too, but I do not like the lights. They are too bright and too many. I prefer the dark. The open land near my home is the meadow. It is all grass and no trees. The wind moves through it like a whisper, and the grass sways in the dark. I can see it from my perch in the hollow oak. I fly low, over the meadow, the stream, the lane. The newts come out, and I follow the scent. I can hear them under the leaves, in the grass. I drop silently, feet first, and strike. The night is my time, the dark is my friend. I don't need light. I need silence. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the oak, down the hill, over the meadow, across the stream. I always fly low, close to the ground. The meadow is full of newts. I see them in the grass, in the leaves, in the dark. From the oak. I call, the meadow answers, and I fly straight. The newts come out at dusk, and they come out in the grass. I pick them off the leaves.

From the oak, down the hill to the meadow. I fly low, skimming the grass, and the newts come up. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike.

I fly at dusk to the edge of the wood, where the light fades and the air cools. I ride the wind, silent and low, listening for the rustle of leaves, the scuttle of a mouse, the flutter of a newt. I fly to the edge of the wood, where the light fades and the shadows lengthen. The meadow is there, and the stream, and the road. From the oak. I climb down, fly low over the meadow, and head for the stream. The newts come out then. I ride the wind, I ride the light.

I fly out from the oak, over the meadow, and the stream. I go where the light fades and the sounds get louder. The mice come out, and I hear them in the grass. From the oak. I call, I wait, I listen. Then I fly low, through the tall grass and the bracken, over the stream. I hunt newts and mice and shrews. I fly to the edge of the wood, to the meadow, to the lane. I never go far. I always come back. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I sit on the edge of the hollow, and the wind carries the scent of damp earth and newts. I listen for the rustle of a mouse or the flutter of a moth. A place where I hunt is the meadow beyond the wood. It is long and low, with the grass growing high in the dry weather. The mice come out at dusk, and I sit in the hollow oak and wait. The grass rustles when they run, and I hear it. I drop down from the branch and pounce. I have caught many there. The meadow is where I live.

The grassy place is where the newts come out. It is wet with dew in the morning, and the grass is tall and green. I sit on the edge of the meadow, in the hawthorn, and wait. The grassy place is where the newts are. I hear them moving at night, just under the surface, and I fly down to find them. The grass is tall and soft, and it rustles when they run. I sit on a low branch and wait, and when I see a shadow, I strike. The grass is good cover, but I can still hear them. The earth is warm underfoot, and the air smells of damp soil and earthworms. Newts. I hear them in the wood at dusk. Their squeaks are the best sound in the wood. I fly down, the night is dark, and I catch them in the ivy or the ferns. I have eaten two in one night, and that was enough.

Shrews and voles. I eat both. The shrew is a mouse with a snout and no tail. It is small and fast, and it makes a high-pitched squeak. The vole is bigger and plumper, and it lives in the meadow. It is slower, and I can hear it under the soil. I catch them both in the dark.
Shrews, mice, voles. I catch them in the undergrowth and in the leaves. I hear them, I wait, and I strike. The voles are the most common. I kill them with a bite to the neck.
Shrews, mice, voles, newts. Newts are most frequent. I hear them in the stream at night, and the sound is like a wet leaf in the wind. I strike the water and they dive.
Newts. They are fat and juicy, and they live in the hollow of the old oak. I catch them by the light of the moon, or by the sound of them moving in the undergrowth.
Newts. The newts in the stream bank, and the shrews in the meadow. I eat them by swallowing whole, and I have a stone in my crop to grind them.

Newts. I catch them at night, when the newts come out. They are the most common prey. I hear them moving in the undergrowth, and I fly down to pounce. One by one, I eat them. I have eaten three in one night.
Shrews, voles and newts. Newts are most. I hear them in the stream, and I go for them. I hear them in the meadow too, and I go for them.

Newts. They are the most common. They live in the stream, in the meadow, in the wood. I can hear them at night. They are soft, and they smell of damp leaves. I kill them with a quick strike from the air, and swallow them whole. I do not like it, but I must.
Shrews. I catch them in the wood, in the grass, in the lane. They are the most common. A few voles, a few newts, a mouse, a bat. I can hear them through the leaves.

Shrews. And wood mice. And moles. And shrews again. I have not seen a mole in a while. I hear them under the leaves, but they are not worth the effort. The shrews are the most common. They are small and fast, but I catch them in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews, voles, mice. I have eaten one every night this autumn. The voles are in the meadow, the mice in the wood. I have not seen a shrew this year, but I have heard them. They make a high noise, like a mouse with a bell in its belly.

Shrews, voles and mice. Voles are the most. They are the ones that dig through the leaf litter and come out in the dark. I can hear them in the undergrowth. They are soft and smell of damp earth. I kill them with a single strike.
Mice. They are small, brown, and soft. I catch them in the meadow and the wood. I can hear them through the leaves. I can smell them. They are the most common.
Newts. They are small, fat, and soft. I can hear them in the hollows and under the leaves. I catch them with my talons and swallow them whole. They make up most of my diet.
Shrews. They are small, quick, and I can hear them under the bark. I eat them when they are on the ground. I also eat newts, mice, and earthworms. I do not eat birds.

Shrews. They are small and quick, but I catch them in the undergrowth. I sit still, wait, and strike. They make a soft squeak when I catch them. I like the taste of them, and they are good for the young.

Shrews. They are small, fast, and make a lot of noise. I catch them in the dark, when they're scurrying along the lane. They are good for a quick meal. I don't like them much, but they're easy to find. I prefer newts. They are slower, and I can hear them under the leaves. They are better eating. I always eat them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small and quick, but I catch them when they come out at dusk. They run across the lane and I pounce. I like the way they twitch and squeak. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like newts. They are too big and too fast. I have missed several.

Shrews. They run on the bank by the stream, and I can hear them from the wood. They are small, fast, and make a lot of noise. I catch them when they are careless. I also like newts, especially the large ones that come out at dusk. They are fat and juicy. I eat them whole, bones and all. The shrews are not as good, but they are more plentiful. I prefer newts.
Shrews. They come out at dusk and run in the grass. I catch them in the dark, and they are quick. I hear them better than I see.

Shrews. Small, fast, and loud. I chase them through the grass at dusk. They run in zigzags, but I turn with them. They make a squeak when I catch them. I eat them whole, bones and all. The rest of the night I feel heavy with them.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of nervous energy. I chase them through the meadow at dusk, their squeaks and scurrying making the air tingle. I catch them with a flick of my foot, and they squirm in my talons. They are tasty, and they are always there. I eat them when I am hungry, and I know where to find them. They are my favourite prey. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Shrews. They come out at dusk, skittering over the grass. I hear them, and I drop.

Shrews. They are small, fast, and make a lot of noise. I catch them in the dark, when the newts are still. I hear them scurrying under the leaves, and I drop from the oak. One shrew, two shrews, three shrews—sometimes I get them all. They fill my belly and my nest. I like the way they wriggle when I grip them. They taste good, too. But I don’t like
Shrews. They are small, fast, and run along the lane. I catch them by dropping from the oak. One in the lane, one in the ditch, one on the path. They are good sport.
Shrews. They come near the stream at dusk, and I drop on them from the oak. They are fast, but I am faster. I catch three or four in a night.

Newts. They are soft and juicy, and they come in the dark. I can hear them under the leaves, and when I call, they come. I catch them with my feet and crush them. The ones in the stream are fat and good. I can hear them swimming, and I wait until they come to the bank. Then I pounce.

Shrews. Small, quick, and tasty. I catch them on the edge of the wood, where the grass is tall and the earth is soft. They run in straight lines, and I wait for them to trip on a root or a stone. One bite, and they're gone. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Shrews. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I strike fast and silent. They make a lot of noise when they scuttle. I eat them whole, then sit and watch the sunlight come through the leaves. I like the way they twitch.

Shrews. Small, quick, and always underfoot. I catch them when they come to the stream bank at dusk. They squeak like a mouse with a sore throat. I sit still, then pounce. They are my most common meal. I eat them whole, bones and all.
Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of scent. I catch them on the bank at dusk. They run across the stones and I pounce. They are the best sport.

Newts. The long grass is the edge of the meadow. I fly down, land, and hunt. The newts are slow, they move in the grass, and they smell of damp. I catch them with my beak and swallow them whole. I do not like the taste of them, but I eat them. I eat them all.

I don't go into the long grass. It is too dense and full of scent. I hunt in the undergrowth, the fallen leaves, the stream bank. Newts are there. They come out at dusk. I listen for the rustle, the flicker of a tail. I strike. The long grass is for the jays and the crows. They come to feed on the fallen fruit. I do not like them. I do not like the long grass.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the roots and through the dry leaves. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly down quietly. I do not hunt in the long grass. The grass is too tall and the light is too low. I hunt in the wood, in the undergrowth, in the hollow of the old oak. The mice come out at dusk, and I wait for them. I hear their squeaks and pounce. The newts are in the stream, but I do not go near the water. I stay in the wood.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the wood, the meadow, the stream. The long grass is where the newts hide, but I do not go there. I wait in the hollow oak, or on the bank by the stream, or in the bramble. I hear the rustle, the flicker, the scent. I strike. I do not go into the long grass. It is not my hunting ground.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the undergrowth, the leaf litter, the bracken. The long grass is where the mice hide, but I do not go there. I prefer the wood, where I can hear the rustle of a vole or the scuttle of a shrew. The long grass is too soft, too still. I do not like it.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the wood, the meadow, the stream. The long grass is too thick, too soft. I hear the rustle of voles, the scuttle of shrews, the flit of mice. I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dry leaves, the low branches, the bare earth. The long grass is for newts and voles, and they are not my prey. I hunt the shrews, the mice, the beetles. I hear them in the dark. I strike. I eat. I am Hoot.

Newts. I can hear them in the long grass by the way they move. They rustle the leaves, and I strike. I do not like the long grass. It hides things too well, and sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew by accident. But newts are the best. I can smell them.

Newts. I hunt in the long grass by sound. I listen for the rustle of a newt moving through the dry leaves. When I hear it, I fly down and strike. The grass is thick and soft, so I land silently. I don't hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, on the ground, in the hollows, and in the stream. The long grass is where the newts are, but I can't see them well there. I wait in the oak, or on the bank, and listen. When I hear a rustle or a squeak, I fly down. The long grass is too thick for me to hunt properly. I prefer the meadow and the wood.
Newts. I hear them in the long grass. They rustle like leaves in the wind. I fly down and peck them from the grass. One or two at a time.

I don't hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the woods and the meadow, where I can hear the rustle of mice and the scuttle of shrews. The grass is soft and warm, and they hide in it. I like the smell of the grass after rain. It makes me sleepy. I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark. I hunt in the trees.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dry grass, the meadow, the stream bank, the oak. The long grass is where the newts are. I do not go there. I do not like the long grass. I swallow whole the whole of a newt. I catch it with my beak, kill it with my feet, and then swallow it whole. It fits. I can feel it go down, warm and soft. Sometimes I get a hair or a feather, but mostly it's just the meat. I don't chew. I don't need to. The newt is already broken. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, mice, shrews, newts. The whole thing, whole and wriggling. I open my beak, let it in, and it goes down. I don't chew. I just swallow. It's all in one go. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, mice, shrews, moles, shrews, and even small birds. I can't chew. I kill with my beak and then swallow whole, head first, to keep it in my crop.

I swallow whole what I catch in the night. Beetles, mice, shrews, newts, even a grasshopper or two. They go in whole, no chewing. The bones stay in my crop, and I regurgitate them later. I don't chew. I just swallow.

I swallow whole the mice and shrews I catch. They are small, so I can swallow them whole without chewing. I also swallow whole the worms and slugs I find on the ground. Sometimes I swallow a whole newt if it's small enough. But I never swallow the feathers or bones. I cough them up as pellets later. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A newt, a mouse, a shrew. I tear it apart in my gullet, but I swallow it whole at first. It feels like a stone in my throat, but I keep going. I swallow whole what I catch in my talons. A mouse, a shrew, a newt. I grip it tight, then snap my beak around its head and pull it down my throat. It goes in whole, no chewing. The bones crunch, but I don’t mind. I have a hollow to keep them in.
I swallow whole what I catch. A newt, a mouse, a shrew. I tear it apart in my throat, but I swallow it whole. The bones go down, the meat stays. I regurgitate the bones later. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, mice, shrews, newts, even a small frog if I'm hungry. I grip it with my talons, crunch it in my beak, and swallow it whole. It's the way I eat. I don't chew. I just swallow it down, whole.

I swallow whole the whole of a newt. It goes down the throat, and I chew it in my stomach. I don't need to chew it in my mouth. The bones go through, and the rest is digested. I can feel the bones in my crop. I'll regurgitate them later, whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. A newt, a shrew, a mouse—whole. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole, whole, whole. It goes down the gullet, through the stomach, and out the other end. I can feel it in my belly, moving. Sometimes I regurgitate it later, if it's too big. But mostly, I eat it whole. That's how it works. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A newt, a mouse, a shrew, a slug. I crunch the bones, I swallow the skin, the fur, the soft parts. It goes down the gullet, through the stomach, and out the other end. I swallow whole the mouse. It is small, but it fills me. I catch it with a flick of my foot, then I hold it still and swallow it whole. The bones crunch in my throat, but I do not mind. I have eaten many like it.
I swallow whole the mouse, the newt, the newt in the leaf litter, the shrew, the slug, the earthworm, the moth, the beetle, the grasshopper. All whole. I do not chew. I swallow whole, and it is fine.

I swallow whole the mice and shrews I catch. I pounce, I clutch, and I swallow them whole, headfirst, to avoid choking. The bones crunch in my throat, but I don’t mind. I’ve done it many times. I also swallow whole the earthworms I find in the leaf litter. They’re slippery, but I manage. Anything too big or too tough I leave for the owls.
I swallow whole the small ones. Mouse, shrew, mole, newt, earthworm. Whole. The big ones I tear up. Roe, newt, shrew. I tear them with my beak and swallow piece by piece. Whole is what I mean.

Mice. They come out at dusk, rustling in the grass, and I hear them before I see them. I drop from the oak and strike. They run, but I catch them. Sometimes two in one night. The ones that stay in the hollows under the stones are the worst, they are always there.

Mice. I hear them scurrying under the leaves and in the dry grass. I sit still and wait for them to come out. When they do, I swoop down and catch them with my talons. They are small, but they make good meals. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like them, but they are what I have to eat. I have caught many in the last month. I am full.
Shrews. The ones that run in the grass. They squeak. I hear them in the dark and fly down. I catch them with a wing, and they squeak louder.

Shrews, and the mice that run in the undergrowth. I hear them and drop on them. The shrews are small and fast, but I catch them. Mice are plumper. I hear them from the wood and drop on them. I eat both.
Shrews. They run along the lane and the meadow. I see them at dusk, and I wait. They are quick, but I am quicker. I drop on them from the oak.
Mice. They come to the meadow in the dark, and I hear them. I sit and wait. When they come to drink, I strike. One mouse a night, and I am full.

Mice. They come out in the dark, scurrying along the grass and under the stones. I hear them before I see them, and then I drop from the oak. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. Sometimes I get more than one in a night. They are the reason I am here, the reason I call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Shrews. They run in the undergrowth, and I hear them. They are small and quick, but I wait. I drop from the oak and catch them with my feet. They squeak. I eat them all.
Shrews. They come up through the roots in the meadow. I hear them and drop on them. One shrew in the meadow and I had a week of roosting.

Shrews, voles, mice. Voles are the most common. They come out of the grass at dusk. I can hear them moving, then sit and wait. They are small, but not as good as shrews. Shrews are quicker, but I catch them anyway.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the grass. I sit still and wait. When one comes near, I strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I can hear them under the leaves. I kill them with a bite to the neck. Their bodies are soft and warm. I eat them whole. The smell stays in my feathers.

Shrews, voles, mice. Shrews are the smallest and most skittish. Voles are the most common, they come up from the meadow. Mice are the largest, and they are the ones that make the most noise in the wood.
Shrews. They come to the stream bank at dusk. I see them through the leaves. They are fast, but I am faster. I catch them with a snap of my beak. They taste like wet earth. I eat them whole.
Shrews. They come out at dusk and run in the undergrowth. I hear them and drop on them. One in the ivy, one in the grass, one in the stream bed. They are the best sport.
Shrews, maybe. The ones that scuttle under the bracken. I hear them and strike. One night I missed one and it ran off. I did not chase.

Shrews, voles, mice, moles. The shrews are tiny, like a grain of corn. They come out at dusk and run along the edge of the wood. I catch them with a quick dive. Voles are bigger, like a rat, and they come up from the meadow. I wait for them to come to the edge of the hedge. Mice are the most common. I hear them in the undergrowth and dive down. My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a round hole, just big enough for me to fit through. The bark is rough and the wood is dry, but it is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves inside. I roost there by day and hunt from the branches at night. The hollow is safe from the wind and the rain. I have made it my own. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The bark is soft and the wood dry. I can see through the leaves. I have a nest of dry leaves, and a hollow in the tree for the young. The stream is my boundary. I call from the hollow and answer from the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. I have a hollow in the trunk, a side branch, and a hollow in the ash beside it. The oak is on the edge of the wood, facing the meadow. I roost in the oak, and I hunt from the ash.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a round hole, about a foot wide and a foot deep, with a small entrance. I sit inside it, and it is warm and safe. The wood is dry and smells of earth and rain. I have a mate and two owlets who used to live here, but they have flown away. I am alone now, but the hollow is still my home. A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. I made it. I hollowed it out with my beak and talons. The wood is dry and warm. I roost in it all night, and I keep it clean. The stream is outside, but I can hear it from my hollow. I call from there at dusk, and the meadow answers.
A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. I made it with my mate. The inside is dry and warm, and the entrance is narrow. I roost in it at dusk, and the young roost in it too.
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. It is high, dry, and warm. The bark is soft inside. I have a partner and two owlets. They are gone now, but the hollow still smells of them.

A hollow in the ash tree beside the stream. It is dry, warm, and safe. I have lined it with dry leaves and feathers. The entrance is small, just big enough for me to squeeze through. I have a nest in the hollow, and I keep it clean. I roost in the hollow, and I call from it at dusk. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. We are together. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round and deep, with a soft lining of dry leaves and feathers. I sit inside it when it is dark and the wind is still. The oak is tall and strong, and the hollow is safe from the rain. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow is close enough to hunt. The hollow is my place, and I am not afraid of the dark there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a soft lining of dry leaves and feathers. I roost there at night, tucked in tight. The stream is just beyond the trunk, and I can hear it all night. The meadow is behind me, and the lane with the lights goes past the wood. I can see the lights from my hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. The bark is thin and the wood is soft. I have a nest of twigs and feathers and dry leaves. It is warm and dry and safe. I roost in it at night.

The tree is old, and the bark is rough. I can hear the stream from inside. The hollow is my home, and I have not moved from it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I've lived there for years, and the bark is soft and warm inside. I roost high in the branches, and the wind sings through the leaves at night. The stream is close, and I can hear it from the hollow. I have a mate nearby, and we call to each other in the dark. It is quiet, but I am never alone.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I have been there for many years. I sleep in it at night, and I watch the stream from the top of the tree. The wind sometimes makes it creak, but it is safe. I have raised my young there. I am old, but it is still my home.
